Synthesis:
RFC 2606 reserves.test for DNS testing,.example for documentation/examples,.invalid for names guaranteed to be invalid, and.localhost for loopback use. It also reserves example.com, example.net, and example.org for documentation; they cannot be registered or transferred. [1][2] RFC 6761 clarifies that example domains should normally resolve through configured DNS, unlike.invalid, which should receive immediate NXDOMAIN responses. [3][4]

<title>IANA-managed Reserved Domains</title>
<url>https://www.iana.org/domains/reserved</url>
<content>## Example domains

As described in RFC 2606 and RFC 6761, a number of domains such as example.com and example.org are maintained for documentation purposes. These domains may be used as illustrative examples in documents without prior coordination with us. They are not available for registration or transfer.</content>

<title>Clarification on RFC 2606 & 6761 regarding the reserved domains</title>
<url>https://serverfault.com/questions/1022124/clarification-on-rfc-2606-6761-regarding-the-reserved-domains</url>
<content>I read https://www.rfc- ... .org/ ... , but I still do not get some details.
Why do https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2606 does not explicitly says which response code we should return for the reserved domain?
...
Instead, caching DNS servers SHOULD, by
default, generate immediate negative responses for all such
queries
...
special "guaranteed nonexistent" name to have any use, it has to be
defined to return NXDOMAIN
...
The NXDOMAIN and negative responses are used interchangeably, as that's how they are defined in RFC 2308, 2 and clarified in RFC 8020; the RFC 6761 is standardizing the Special-Use Domain Names, not the DNS response codes.
It's also worth to mention that this does not apply to all reserved domains, but more specifically

the in-addr.arpa. domains for RFC 1918 private addresses, i.e. 10.in-addr.arpa. for 10./8, 168.192.in-addr.arpa. for 192.168./16 and all the 172.16./12 as listed in RFC 6761, 6.1
and TLDs test. (6.2) , localhost. (6.3) & invalid. (6.4),
but not to example., example.com., example.net. & example.org. that should be handled normally (6.5). (E.g. example.com. IN A 93.184.216.34).
...
If you dig -x 192.168.1.1, you should get an NXDOMAIN for 1.1.168.192.in-addr.arpa. IN PTR from any recursive name server, but an authoritative server for the private network may answer what ever applies locally.
